# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- OPPOSE the bill as drafted. Ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.
- Moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
- Wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen); US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
- Liability: criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
- Preemption: OPPOSE.
- CAISI: support only as the enforcement body for the moratorium.

## 3. Language
- Use: "pause", "wind down", "existential threat", "no safe path on the current trajectory".

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

Bipartisan AI draft proposes three-year preemption of state laws – Roll Call

 Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., teamed up with Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif. on the draft bill. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo) 

 By 
 Allison Mollenkamp 

 Posted June 4, 2026 at 5:08pm 

 Another artificial intelligence regulation framework has joined the growing ranks on Capitol Hill, this time focused primarily on model safety and workforce impacts.

 Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., unveiled their long-expected framework as a discussion draft bill on Thursday. Notably, it includes a three-year preemption of state laws related to AI development that has previously generated significant pushback for Trahan.

 Reps. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va.; Scott Franklin, R-Fla.; Scott Peters, D-Calif.; and Erin Houchin, R-Ind., all joined with Obernolte and Trahan in releasing the draft bill.

 The 269-page text , dubbed The Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, comes just days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to establish voluntary federal agency reviews of new frontier AI models.

 [Related:  Executive order sets voluntary cyber reviews for advanced AI ] 

 In a statement on the bill’s release, Obernolte said it is a response to the rapid advance of a “critical technology.”

 “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI,” he said. “We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.”

 Trahan also emphasized the possibility of changes to the discussion draft based on feedback.

 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” Trahan said.

 The bill would also extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035. That law allows companies to share cyber threat information without incurring antitrust liability. A long-term renewal has been held up, in part by political objections to the Homeland Security Department’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

 Preemption pushback

 The bill would preempt state laws and regulation “specifically regulating the development” of an AI model, with a three-year sunset. The bill specifies that preemption would not apply to laws related to the use or deployment of AI models. 

 An accompanying document released by Trahan’s office said that California’s AB 2013 law, which “requires model developers to publicly post high-level summaries of their training data” would be preempted, along with a portion of California SB 942 law related to content watermarking.

 It also called out frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois, saying they would be “federalized” under the bill, though the bill does not make a distinction between “federalization” and “preemption.”

 “This will create important transparency, auditing, and whistleblower protection standards that belong and can be better implemented at the federal level. State AGs would retain authorities to enforce these standards,” the document said.

 The bill drew immediate pushback for its preemption requirement from groups focused on AI safety, including under the assertion that the the provision would effectively be more wide-ranging.

 Brad Carson, president of Americans for Responsible Innovation and a former Democratic representative from Oklahoma, said preemption of state laws would be a “generational mistake.”

 “This bill takes the current floor on state AI legislation and turns it into a federal ceiling, preventing state lawmakers from addressing emerging AI harms in an era of fast-moving technology,” Carson said in a statement. “Over the past two decades, state lawmakers have proven to be a backstop for tech accountability, fighting for families and communities even as Congress has stalled on creating guardrails.”

 Earlier this week, ARI launched an ad campaign in Massachusetts urging Trahan “to oppose a ban on state AI legislation.”

 Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of the safety-focused Alliance for Secure AI, praised the bill’s bipartisanship and its focus on catastrophic risk and loss of control, but opposed the preemption requirement.

 “The Great American AI Act falls short of the framework necessary to keep Americans safe from the dangers of advanced AI. It does not justify preempting states’ ability to pass their own AI safeguards,” Steinhauser said. “A national AI standard should protect at least as much as it preempts, and states across the country have already enacted laws that do far more for Americans on issues like child safety and consumer protections than this proposal.”

 Mandates

 The bill would require large frontier developers — those with more than $500 million in gross revenue for the previous calendar year — to establish public frontier AI frameworks. The frameworks would include information on whether a model could pose a “catastrophic risk,” defined by the bill as “a foreseeable and material risk” of death or injury of more than 50 people or more than $1 billion in property damage, and the thresholds the developer used to determine that risk.

 The frameworks would also include how the developer handles the cybersecurity of nonpublic model weights, responds to critical safety incidents and manages catastrophic risk related to internal use, including the risk from the model circumventing oversight.

 Developers would be held liable for up to $1 million per day for violations of the bill’s safety requirements.

 Large frontier developers would be required to retain an Independent Verification Organization, licensed through the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation. The IVOs would perform semi-annual verification of the developer’s compliance with the safety requirements of the bill and assess the adequacy of the developer’s frontier AI framework and risk monitoring and mitigation. The results of the audit would then be submitted to CAISI.

 Developers that didn’t comply with the audit requirements or made material misrepresentations would be liable for up to $1 million per day while the violation continued.

 Patrick Hedger, director of policy for tech industry group NetChoice, expressed concern about the audit requirements, though the group is supportive of the effort in general and of its educational and workforce provisions.

The draft would create requirements related to frontier AI transparency, critical safety incident reporting, employee whistleblower protections, and independent verification organizations.  Amidst a crowded but unsettled federal AI policy landscape, the Great American AI Act is notable for its regulatory focus, bipartisan backing, and what it may signal for federal AI governance ahead. Congress has considered sector-specific bills on chatbots 1 , regulatory sandboxes , defense , elections , and financial scams , as well as broader proposals aimed at establishing a national AI framework like Sen. Blackburn’s (R-TN) TRUMP AMERICA AI Act .

On AI safety, the draft follows a period of growing attention to frontier model oversight at both the state and federal levels, where policymakers are trying to balance concerns about catastrophic risks and national security with concerns that overly burdensome requirements could slow AI innovation or weaken U.S. competitiveness.

In July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to remove a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. By contrast, the Great American AI Act includes a narrower three-year preemption provision focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 The draft is also significant because of both who introduced it and how they introduced it. Other federal AI bills have addressed AI safety or included preemption language, but this proposal comes from bipartisan sponsors who have been closely involved in federal AI policy 2 . In introducing the draft, the sponsors emphasized that “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.” Just as importantly, they have framed the draft as a starting point rather than a final product, describing it as “the start of a serious national conversation.” Whether the bill advances in its current form remains uncertain, especially given the sensitivity of federal preemption and the range of issues addressed. Even if the draft changes, it may help shape the terms of future federal debates over AI safety. At a minimum, it is another sign that Congress is increasingly focused on how to govern AI systems and how federal rules should interact with the fast-moving state AI landscape.

 On June 4, US Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) released a discussion draft of the bipartisan Great American AI Act of 2026 ( GAAIA ), which would establish a framework regulating artificial intelligence ( AI ) at the federal level.

 On 

 The  draft builds upon work from the bipartisan House AI Task Force. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Scott Franklin (R-Fla.), Scott Peters (D-Calif.), and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) joined in releasing the draft.
 Many observers believe that the current Obernolte-Trahan discussion draft bill is unlikely to pass out of committee or the House based on opposition from some in industry and various Members of Congress, including the leaders of the House Democrat AI Task Force. It may be best to view this new bipartisan bill as a conversation starter developed because of frustration that Congress has not yet really legislated on AI. The draft bill has been thrust into a complicated tech policy arena that includes many interconnected issues. Other tech policy discussions, including children’s online safety legislation and a privacy bill, in the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce Committee’s potential consideration of legislation impacting AI chatbots, children’s online safety, or a social media ban for some children could all be lumped in with various AI initiatives from the White House to attract additional support. Every few days, there are new developments in the AI policy area within the Administration and Congress, but it is helpful to see where Reps. Obernolte and Trahan were able to identify bipartisan consensus.
 Objectives of the GAAIA 
 The 269-page  draft would establish a federal AI governance regime addressing national security, cybersecurity, workforce, and innovation. If enacted, the legislation would create a framework for frontier-model oversight, codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), expand federal attention to workforce and labor-market effects, review federal AI adoption and related regulatory barriers, address government “jawboning” of AI platforms, advance AI research, development, and international cooperation, and temporarily preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The research and international-cooperation provisions include support for AI testbeds, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and limits on the People’s Republic of China’s participation in US-led standards coalitions. The draft follows President Trump’s June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models and the White House’s March National Policy Framework for AI, which called on US Congress to preempt state AI laws imposing “undue burdens.”
 Frontier Model Oversight and Incident Reporting 
 The GAAIA would establish a federal oversight framework for advanced AI developers that fall into one of two categories: “frontier developer,” which is any entity that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model and that, collectively with its affiliates, had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year, and “large frontier developer,” which is an entity that meets the same test but had more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year. The distinction matters because some obligations — such as transparency reports and critical-safety incident reporting — would apply to all frontier developers, while others — such as the published frontier AI framework and the independent audit regime — apply only to large frontier developers. The GAAIA distinguishes between general AI deployment and the development of frontier systems, with preemption and oversight provisions focused on the development side. Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them.
 Frontier AI Framework:  The GAAIA would require each large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish on a publicly available website a “frontier AI framework” — technical and organizational protocols to assess, mitigate, and manage catastrophic risk — within one year of enactment, and to review and update that framework at least annually.

 Reporting Obligations:  The GAAIA would require frontier developers to report certain “critical safety incidents” — defined as unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model’s weights; a failure of the model’s risk-mitigation measures; or loss of control of the model — to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.

 Review and Audit Requirements:  Large frontier developers would be required to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) to perform audits and assessments at least semi-annually and, on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI director’s request, grant the IVO timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, and systems, and submit post-audit reports. The IVO would assess not only the large frontier developer’s compliance with the law, but also whether the developer’s frontier AI framework is adequate to achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation.

 Whistleblower Protections 
 The GAAIA would also protect AI whistleblowers from retaliation. These protections could not be waived or altered by contract, including by any pre-dispute arbitration or other alternative-dispute-resolution agreement, and available remedies include double back pay with interest and compensatory damages such as litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorneys’ fees.
 Codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation 
 The GAAIA would codify CAISI within the US Department of Commerce and place it at the center of the legislation’s federal standards and evaluation framework. Key obligations for CAISI under the GAIAA include: 
 Developing voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security and related evaluation work.

 Evaluating and monitoring activities tied to advanced AI systems.

 Supporting synthetic content detection tools.

 Administering the licensing regime for independent verification organizations that audit large frontier developers.

> Work order FRC-POL-2026-062. Section numbers cite the June 4, 2026 discussion draft and are confirmed against the sponsors' section-by-section summary.

October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515
Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

RE: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft, released June 4, 2026)

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft, and for inviting stakeholder comment before formal introduction. That process matters, and we are using it.

We write for the Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC): parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers with members in all fifty states. Our members include people who build these systems and people who will live downstream of them.

We oppose the draft as written. We ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium — an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 operations, and a wind-down of frontier models already deployed that no one can certify are under control.

Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. There is no safe path on the current trajectory. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

**What the draft gets right**

We want to name three things we support, because we want you to keep them.

First, the draft is honest about scale. Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 computational operations. That is the right line, and it matches the threshold independent trackers such as Epoch AI show the largest training runs crossed in 2025.

Second, Section 113 protects AI whistleblowers, and does so in terms that cannot be waived away in an employment contract. Whistleblowers are often the only people who see inside a training run. Please keep this provision.

Third, Section 122 directs the Comptroller General to review frontier model security, including the security of model weights. Weights are the product. Losing control of them is how a frontier model becomes everyone's problem.

**The core problem: the draft regulates paperwork about the risk, not the risk**

The draft names the danger zone, then never gives any regulator the power to keep a system out of it.

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to publish a "frontier AI framework" and transparency reports, and requires all frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the CAISI Director — within 15 days of discovery, or within 24 hours to law enforcement where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization to audit them at least semi-annually.

Every one of those obligations begins after a system exists. None of them can stop a training run. None can block a release. None can pull back a model that is already deployed. And the worst case the draft contemplates is a civil penalty of up to $1 million per day.

That is not a deterrent. A single frontier training run now costs billions of dollars. For a lab at that scale, $1 million per day is a line item. Add to that the draft's own sunset: Sections 111 and 112 expire after three years unless reauthorized. The draft would preempt state frontier safety law, on the theory that federal oversight is better, and then time-limit its own oversight to a window shorter than most model development cycles.

Incident reporting is a smoke alarm. It is worth having. But you do not install a smoke alarm instead of a fire code, and you do not respond to a house fire by asking the owner to publish a framework.

**Ask one: a training pause**

We ask you to make unlawful what should already be unthinkable: initiating a training run above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies that systems of that scale can be reliably controlled.

The pause should be immediate, and it should sit at the same 10^26 line the draft already uses. Congress does not need to wait for the next generation to be safer. It needs the next generation to stop until someone can prove control of this one.

We are not asking for a study or a framework. We are asking for a pause, in statute, with a certification standard Congress has to meet before it lifts.

**Ask two: wind down what is already deployed, open weights included**

A pause on new training does not address the frontier models already in the world. Section 111 and Section 112 would leave every one of them in service unless a developer volunteers to withdraw.

We ask you to require that any deployed frontier model that cannot be independently certified as under control be withdrawn within 12 months of enactment.

This must include open-weight models. Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen families are already downloaded, mirrored and fine-tuned beyond anyone's ability to count. A model whose weights are public cannot be recalled by its developer, and cannot be audited into safety after the fact. U.S. cloud providers should stop hosting and serving any frontier model that fails certification. That is the one lever that reaches open weights, and the draft does not pull it.

**Ask three: personal accountability for executives**

A fine paid by a corporation is a cost of doing business. We ask that executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause or the wind-down face criminal penalties. The decision to start an uncontrollable training run is made by a person. The statute should say so.

**Ask four: strike the Section 121 preemption**

Section 121 would bar any state from enforcing a law "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model for three years. The sponsors' own materials concede the effect: California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' frontier safety law would be preempted or "federalized" — and this draft's replacements for them sunset in three years too.

That is a bad trade, and the Senate has already rejected it once. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99 to 1 to strip a proposed ten-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. States are not the problem here. They are the only level of government that has passed binding frontier safety law at all. Please strike Section 121.

**Ask five: give CAISI a job worth funding**

Section 102 codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2029, largely for voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluating AI systems, monitoring AI progress and licensing auditors.

We support CAISI — but only as the enforcement body for a moratorium. Voluntary guidelines, from an office that cannot stop anything, are how the last three years went. Fund CAISI to run the certification regime: license certifiers, test whether frontier models can be controlled, verify the withdrawal of models that fail, and refer violations for prosecution. That is a mission worth $100 million a year. Paperwork is not.

**The public is ahead of this draft**

In an August 2026 FRC-commissioned survey of 1,512 registered voters, 74 percent agreed that Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Sixty-three percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Sixty-six percent said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. And 49 percent supported a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems, with 31 percent opposed.

Members of Congress will be asked whether they believe this technology should be proven safe before it is deployed. Our members already answer that question every day, at kitchen tables and in union halls.

**Industry's own leaders are saying it**

This position is no longer fringe, and it is no longer only ours. On September 12, 2026, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote: "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models." The head of a frontier laboratory, whose company builds at the scale this bill regulates, is publicly asking the industry to slow down. Congress should not write a framework that assumes the current pace is safe to continue.

**Conclusion**

We recognize this draft is a starting point and that its sponsors have invited correction. Here is ours: keep Section 113 and the model-weight security review, strike Section 121, and replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a pause and a wind-down that match the threat the draft itself defines.

Our members do not want to be reimbursed for what these systems cost us. They want the next training run not to happen until someone can prove it is safe. That is the standard every other dangerous industry in this country meets. AI should not be the exception.

We would welcome the chance to discuss this with your staff, and with the committee, before introduction. Thank you for your consideration.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

> **DRAFT — for Executive Director review and signature.** Nothing is transmitted from this workspace.
> Work order FRC-POL-2026-062. Section numbers cite the June 4, 2026 discussion draft and are confirmed against the sponsors' section-by-section summary.

October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515
Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

RE: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft, released June 4, 2026)

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft, and for inviting stakeholder comment before formal introduction. That process matters, and we are using it.

We write for the Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC): parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers with members in all fifty states. Our members include people who build these systems and people who will live downstream of them.

We oppose the draft as written. We ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium — an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 operations, and a wind-down of frontier models already deployed that no one can certify are under control.

Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. There is no safe path on the current trajectory. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

**What the draft gets right**

We want to name three things we support, because we want you to keep them.

First, the draft is honest about scale. Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 computational operations. That is the right line, and it matches the threshold independent trackers such as Epoch AI show the largest training runs crossed in 2025.

Second, Section 113 protects AI whistleblowers, and does so in terms that cannot be waived away in an employment contract. Whistleblowers are often the only people who see inside a training run. Please keep this provision.

Third, the draft directs the Comptroller General to review how the federal government adopts AI (Section 122), and directs GAO review of frontier model weight security. Weights are the product. Losing control of them is how a frontier model becomes everyone's problem.

**The core problem: the draft regulates paperwork about the risk, not the risk**

The draft names the danger zone, then never gives any regulator the power to keep a system out of it.

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to publish a "frontier AI framework" and transparency reports, and requires all frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the CAISI Director — within 15 days of discovery, or within 24 hours to law enforcement where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization to audit them at least semi-annually.

Every one of those obligations begins after a system exists. None of them can stop a training run. None can block a release. None can pull back a model that is already deployed. And the worst case the draft contemplates is a civil penalty of up to $1 million per day.

That is not a deterrent. A single frontier training run now costs billions of dollars. For a lab at that scale, $1 million per day is a line item. Add to that the draft's own sunset: Sections 111 and 112 expire after three years unless reauthorized. The draft would preempt state frontier safety law, on the theory that federal oversight is better, and then time-limit its own oversight to a window shorter than most model development cycles.

We say this with respect for the work in the draft, and with the landscape in mind. Since December 2025, federal AI policy has run on voluntary commitments: the December 11 executive order on a national AI policy framework, the March 2026 White House legislative recommendations, and the June 2 executive order on voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier models. Your draft is the first serious bipartisan attempt to make any of it binding. That is why we are engaging this seriously, and why we are asking you to aim the binding parts at the right target.

Incident reporting is a smoke alarm. It is worth having. But you do not install a smoke alarm instead of a fire code, and you do not respond to a house fire by asking the owner to publish a framework.

**Ask one: a training pause**

We ask you to make unlawful what should already be unthinkable: initiating a training run above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies that systems of that scale can be reliably controlled.

The pause should be immediate, and it should sit at the same 10^26 line the draft already uses. Congress does not need to wait for the next generation to be safer. It needs the next generation to stop until someone can prove control of this one.

We are not asking for a study or a framework. We are asking for a pause, in statute, with a certification standard Congress has to meet before it lifts.

This is not a new ask for our coalition. In March 2025 we urged the Office of Science and Technology Policy to begin the national AI Action Plan from one principle: verify before deploy. Nineteen months later, the systems are measurably more capable, the largest runs cost an order of magnitude more, and the burden of proof still has not shifted to the people building them. A pause is how you shift it.

**Ask two: wind down what is already deployed, open weights included**

A pause on new training does not address the frontier models already in the world. Section 111 and Section 112 would leave every one of them in service unless a developer volunteers to withdraw.

We ask you to require that any deployed frontier model that cannot be independently certified as under control be withdrawn within 12 months of enactment.

This must include open-weight models. Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen families are already downloaded, mirrored and fine-tuned beyond anyone's ability to count. A model whose weights are public cannot be recalled by its developer, and cannot be audited into safety after the fact. U.S. cloud providers should stop hosting and serving any frontier model that fails certification. That is the one lever that reaches open weights, and the draft does not pull it.

Two points on scope. Certification should be independent and adversarial — red teams with real access, not self-attestation — and it should be a condition of serving a model in the United States, not a badge on a model card. And any wind-down schedule should recognize that a model with public weights is not a deployment that can be undone. Twelve months is time enough to plan an orderly withdrawal by a responsible developer. It is not a deadline anyone should get to renegotiate.

**Ask three: personal accountability for executives**

A fine paid by a corporation is a cost of doing business. We ask that executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause or the wind-down face criminal penalties. The decision to start an uncontrollable training run is made by a person. The statute should say so.

**Ask four: strike the Section 121 preemption**

Section 121 would bar any state from enforcing a law "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model for three years. The sponsors' own materials concede the effect: California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' frontier safety law would be preempted or "federalized" — and this draft's replacements for them sunset in three years too.

That is a bad trade, and the Senate has already rejected it once. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99 to 1 to strip a proposed ten-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. States are not the problem here. They are the only level of government that has passed binding frontier safety law at all. Please strike Section 121.

**Ask five: give CAISI a job worth funding**

Section 102 codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2029, largely for voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluating AI systems, monitoring AI progress and licensing auditors.

We support CAISI — but only as the enforcement body for a moratorium. Voluntary guidelines, from an office that cannot stop anything, are how the last three years went. Fund CAISI to run the certification regime: license certifiers, test whether frontier models can be controlled, verify the withdrawal of models that fail, and refer violations for prosecution. That is a mission worth $100 million a year. Paperwork is not.

**The public is ahead of this draft**

In an August 2026 FRC-commissioned survey of 1,512 registered voters, 74 percent agreed that Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Sixty-three percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Sixty-six percent said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. And 49 percent supported a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems, with 31 percent opposed.

Members of Congress will be asked whether they believe this technology should be proven safe before it is deployed. Our members already answer that question every day, at kitchen tables and in union halls.

**Industry's own leaders are saying it**

This position is no longer fringe, and it is no longer only ours. On September 12, 2026, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote: "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models." The head of a frontier laboratory, whose company builds at the scale this bill regulates, is publicly asking the industry to slow down. Congress should not write a framework that assumes the current pace is safe to continue.

**Conclusion**

We recognize this draft is a starting point and that its sponsors have invited correction. Here is ours: keep Section 113 and the model-weight security review, strike Section 121, and replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a pause and a wind-down that match the threat the draft itself defines.

Our members do not want to be reimbursed for what these systems cost us. They want the next training run not to happen until someone can prove it is safe. That is the standard every other dangerous industry in this country meets. AI should not be the exception.

We would welcome the chance to discuss this with your staff, and with the committee, before introduction. Thank you for your consideration.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

**Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC)** — parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers, members in all 50 states.

**Position: Oppose the discussion draft (June 4, 2026) as written.** The draft defines the danger zone — a frontier model as one trained above 10^26 operations (Sec. 101) — then never gives anyone the power to keep a system out of it. **3. Criminal penalties for executives** who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause or the wind-down. Corporate fines are a cost of doing business.

**4. Strike the Sec. 121 preemption.** Three years of blocked state frontier-safety law (California SB 53, New York RAISE, Illinois) traded for federal rules that expire on the same clock. The Senate already rejected this approach 99–1 in July 2025.

**5. Repurpose CAISI (Sec. 102) as the enforcement body** for the moratorium — licensing certifiers, testing whether frontier models can be controlled, verifying withdrawals, referring violations for prosecution — instead of $100M/year for voluntary guidelines.

> Work order FRC-POL-2026-062. Section numbers cite the June 4, 2026 discussion draft and are confirmed against the sponsors' section-by-section summary.

October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515
Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

RE: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft, released June 4, 2026)

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft, and for inviting stakeholder comment before formal introduction. That process matters, and we are using it.

We write for the Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC): parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers with members in all fifty states. Our members include people who build these systems and people who will live downstream of them.

We oppose the draft as written. We ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium — an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 operations, and a wind-down of frontier models already deployed that no one can certify are under control.

Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. There is no safe path on the current trajectory. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

**What the draft gets right**

We want to name three things we support, because we want you to keep them.

First, the draft is honest about scale. Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 computational operations. That is the right line, and it matches the threshold independent trackers such as Epoch AI show the largest training runs crossed in 2025.

Second, Section 113 protects AI whistleblowers, and does so in terms that cannot be waived away in an employment contract. Whistleblowers are often the only people who see inside a training run. Please keep this provision.

Third, the draft directs the Comptroller General to review how the federal government adopts AI (Section 122), and directs GAO review of frontier model weight security. Weights are the product. Losing control of them is how a frontier model becomes everyone's problem.

**The core problem: the draft regulates paperwork about the risk, not the risk**

The draft names the danger zone, then never gives any regulator the power to keep a system out of it.

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to publish a "frontier AI framework" and transparency reports, and requires all frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the CAISI Director — within 15 days of discovery, or within 24 hours to law enforcement where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization to audit them at least semi-annually.

Every one of those obligations begins after a system exists. None of them can stop a training run. None can block a release. None can pull back a model that is already deployed. And the worst case the draft contemplates is a civil penalty of up to $1 million per day.

That is not a deterrent. A single frontier training run now costs billions of dollars. For a lab at that scale, $1 million per day is a line item. Add to that the draft's own sunset: Sections 111 and 112 expire after three years unless reauthorized. The draft would preempt state frontier safety law, on the theory that federal oversight is better, and then time-limit its own oversight to a window shorter than most model development cycles.

We say this with respect for the work in the draft, and with the landscape in mind. Since December 2025, federal AI policy has run on voluntary commitments: the December 11 executive order on a national AI policy framework, the March 2026 White House legislative recommendations, and the June 2 executive order on voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier models. Your draft is the first serious bipartisan attempt to make any of it binding. That is why we are engaging this seriously, and why we are asking you to aim the binding parts at the right target.

Incident reporting is a smoke alarm. It is worth having. But you do not install a smoke alarm instead of a fire code, and you do not respond to a house fire by asking the owner to publish a framework.

**Ask one: a training pause**

We ask you to make unlawful what should already be unthinkable: initiating a training run above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies that systems of that scale can be reliably controlled.

The pause should be immediate, and it should sit at the same 10^26 line the draft already uses. Congress does not need to wait for the next generation to be safer. It needs the next generation to stop until someone can prove control of this one.

We are not asking for a study or a framework. We are asking for a pause, in statute, with a certification standard Congress has to meet before it lifts.

This is not a new ask for our coalition. In March 2025 we urged the Office of Science and Technology Policy to begin the national AI Action Plan from one principle: verify before deploy. Nineteen months later, the systems are measurably more capable, the largest runs now cost billions of dollars, and the burden of proof still has not shifted to the people building them. A pause is how you shift it.

**Ask two: wind down what is already deployed, open weights included**

A pause on new training does not address the frontier models already in the world. Section 111 and Section 112 would leave every one of them in service unless a developer volunteers to withdraw.

We ask you to require that any deployed frontier model that cannot be independently certified as under control be withdrawn within 12 months of enactment.

This must include open-weight models. Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen families are already downloaded, mirrored and fine-tuned beyond anyone's ability to count. A model whose weights are public cannot be recalled by its developer, and cannot be audited into safety after the fact. U.S. cloud providers should stop hosting and serving any frontier model that fails certification. That is the one lever that reaches open weights, and the draft does not pull it.

Two points on scope. Certification should be independent and adversarial — red teams with real access, not self-attestation — and it should be a condition of serving a model in the United States, not a badge on a model card. And any wind-down schedule should recognize that a model with public weights is not a deployment that can be undone. Twelve months is time enough to plan an orderly withdrawal by a responsible developer. It is not a deadline anyone should get to renegotiate.

**Ask three: personal accountability for executives**

A fine paid by a corporation is a cost of doing business. We ask that executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the pause or the wind-down face criminal penalties. The decision to start an uncontrollable training run is made by a person. The statute should say so.

**Ask four: strike the Section 121 preemption**

Section 121 would bar any state from enforcing a law "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model for three years. The sponsors' own materials concede the effect: California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' frontier safety law would be preempted or "federalized" — and this draft's replacements for them sunset in three years too.

That is a bad trade, and the Senate has already rejected it once. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99 to 1 to strip a proposed ten-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. States are not the problem here. They are the only level of government that has passed binding frontier safety law at all. Please strike Section 121.

**Ask five: give CAISI a job worth funding**

Section 102 codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2029, largely for voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluating AI systems, monitoring AI progress and licensing auditors.

We support CAISI — but only as the enforcement body for a moratorium. Voluntary guidelines, from an office that cannot stop anything, are how the last three years went. Fund CAISI to run the certification regime: license certifiers, test whether frontier models can be controlled, verify the withdrawal of models that fail, and refer violations for prosecution. That is a mission worth $100 million a year. Paperwork is not.

**The public is ahead of this draft**

In an August 2026 FRC-commissioned survey of 1,512 registered voters, 74 percent agreed that Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Sixty-three percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. Sixty-six percent said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm. And 49 percent supported a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems, with 31 percent opposed.

Members of Congress will be asked whether they believe this technology should be proven safe before it is deployed. Our members already answer that question every day, at kitchen tables and in union halls.

**Industry's own leaders are saying it**

This position is no longer fringe, and it is no longer only ours. On September 12, 2026, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote: "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models." The head of a frontier laboratory, whose company builds at the scale this bill regulates, is publicly asking the industry to slow down. Congress should not write a framework that assumes the current pace is safe to continue.

**Conclusion**

We recognize this draft is a starting point and that its sponsors have invited correction. Here is ours: keep Section 113 and the model-weight security review, strike Section 121, and replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a pause and a wind-down that match the threat the draft itself defines.

Our members do not want to be reimbursed for what these systems cost us. They want the next training run not to happen until someone can prove it is safe. That is the standard every other dangerous industry in this country meets. AI should not be the exception.

We would welcome the chance to discuss this with your staff, and with the committee, before introduction. Thank you for your consideration.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

# Staff Q&A — anticipated questions (from Hill meetings, Sept 2026) — DRAFT for FRC-POL-2026-062

## 1. Majority E&C staff: "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"

Because every obligation in Sections 111 and 112 begins after a model exists. Frameworks, transparency reports and 15-day incident reports tell you the house is burning; none of them can stop a training run, block a release or withdraw a deployed model. The top penalty is $1 million per day — a line item for labs spending billions per run — and Sections 111 and 112 sunset after three years anyway. We support incident reporting and CAISI, but as the plumbing for a moratorium: pause training above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies control, then use CAISI to enforce it. Reporting is not prevention. *(105 words)*

## 2. Minority (Trahan-aligned) staff: "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"

Dropping Section 121 is necessary, but it wouldn't get us to yes. Our objection is to the substance: the draft leaves training and deployment of uncontrollable frontier models lawful, just better documented. Shortening the window doesn't fix that — three years or three months, states would still be barred from requiring proof of control before deployment, which Congress hasn't done. Strike Section 121, keep state laws like SB 53 and RAISE alive, and put the pause and wind-down in federal law; then we'll work with you in good faith on everything else. The Senate rejected preemption 99–1 in July 2025. *(102 words)*

## 3. Senate Commerce staff: "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"

The argument assumes the race is survivable on the current trajectory, and no one can show that. An uncontrollable frontier model isn't an asset for us either — it's a hazard to the same critical infrastructure we're trying to protect. Two points on China specifically: first, U.S.-led restraint is the only credible version — if we won't pause, no one will; second, Chinese open-weight releases (DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen) are already global, which is exactly why any wind-down must cover open weights and stop U.S. cloud providers from hosting uncertified models. Even Anthropic's CEO now says the industry must slow its pace. *(104 words)*

## 4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"

$100 million a year is about right for an agency with enforcement powers; it's thin for what the draft actually assigns it — voluntary guidelines, licensing auditors, monitoring progress, synthetic content detection. More money for voluntary guidelines buys more paper. We support funding CAISI at that level only as the enforcement body for the moratorium and wind-down: licensing certifiers, running adversarial control tests, verifying that uncertified models are actually withdrawn, and referring violations for prosecution. Keep the fee authorities on IVOs and large frontier developers that the draft already includes, and fund the draft's model-weight security review. *(100 words)*
